CRYPTOGRAPHY ALGORITHMS AT A GLANCE
Symmetric encryption
A shared secret key protects the message. AES is a block cipher. ECB, CBC and CTR are ways to
use it on a longer message.
Building blocks and ciphers
PRG
A pseudorandom generator stretches a short random seed into a longer
sequence of bits that looks random.
PRF
A pseudorandom function is a keyed function whose outputs look random.
Different inputs can give the same output.
PRP
A pseudorandom permutation is a keyed, reversible shuffle of the input
space. AES is modeled as a PRP.
One-time pad (OTP)
XORs a message with a truly random secret pad of the same length. Gives
perfect secrecy when the pad is used once.
Stream cipher
Generates a keystream and XORs it with the message. The same XOR
operation decrypts it. Keystream reuse leaks information.
RC4 / CSS
Historical examples of stream encryption. RC4 was used in network
protocols and CSS was used for DVDs. Both have known weaknesses.
Salsa20 / ChaCha20
Stream ciphers that generate keystream from a key, nonce and counter.
eSTREAM was a project that evaluated stream ciphers.
AES
Encrypts one 16-byte block at a time with a 128-, 192- or 256-bit key. A
mode determines how to handle longer messages.
3DES / Blowfish
Older block ciphers with 64-bit blocks. 3DES applies DES three times.
Blowfish is a separate block cipher.
Modes and padding
ECB
Encrypts each block independently. Equal plaintext blocks give equal
ciphertext blocks, revealing patterns.
CBC
XORs each plaintext block with the previous ciphertext block before
encrypting it. The first block uses a fresh, unpredictable IV.
Deterministic CTR
Encrypts fixed counter values to generate a keystream. The slide version is
for one message per key because restarting repeats the stream.
Nonce-based CTR
Encrypts nonce-and-counter blocks to generate a keystream. Counter inputs
must never repeat under a key. Handles partial blocks without padding.
PKCS#5 / PKCS#7 padding
Fills the last block by repeating the number of added bytes. Add a full
padding block if the message already fits. Java calls the AES version
PKCS5Padding.
CBC needs an unpredictable IV. CTR needs unique counter inputs. The IV or nonce can travel with
the ciphertext.
Deck 1, slides 5-39. ChaCha20 and PKCS padding are from the course discussion.

CRYPTOGRAPHY ALGORITHMS AT A GLANCE
Hashes and message authentication
A hash produces a digest. A message authentication code (MAC) uses a shared secret to produce
a tag the receiver can verify.
Hashes and compression
CRC
Computes a checksum for detecting accidental errors. Anyone can
recompute it after altering a message.
MD5 / SHA-1
Older hashes with 128- and 160-bit digests, respectively. Both have known
collision attacks.
SHA-2
Hash family that includes SHA-256 and SHA-512. The numbers give the
digest length in bits.
SHA-3 / Whirlpool
SHA-3 is a hash family based on a sponge construction. Whirlpool is a
separate hash with a 512-bit digest.
Merkle-Damgård
Pads the message and processes it one block at a time. Each block updates
a running state, and the final state gives the hash.
Davies-Meyer
Uses the message block as a block-cipher key, encrypts the old state and
XORs the result with the old state.
Matyas-Meyer-Oseas
Uses the old state to form a key, encrypts the message block and XORs the
result with that block.
Miyaguchi-Preneel
Uses the old state to form a key, encrypts the message block and XORs the
result with both the block and the old state.
SHA-256 compression
Updates a 256-bit state for each 512-bit message block. The slides show its
Davies-Meyer-style connection to SHACAL-2.
Birthday collision search
Looks for any two different messages with the same hash. For an ideal n-bit
hash, a collision becomes likely after about 2^(n/2) hashes.
Tag generation
PRF-based MAC
Uses the output of a keyed pseudorandom function as the tag. Shortening
the tag makes it easier to guess.
CBC-MAC
Chains message blocks from a fixed zero starting value and uses the final
state as the tag. Basic CBC-MAC is for fixed-length messages.
ECBC-MAC
Encrypts the final CBC-MAC state again with a second independent key.
Supports variable numbers of full blocks.
Hash-then-MAC
Hashes a long message and applies a short-input MAC to the digest. The
slide example applies two-block AES-CBC-MAC to SHA-256.
HMAC
Uses an inner and outer keyed hash with fixed constants called ipad and
opad. The outer hash protects the inner state from simple length extension.
A trusted published digest can verify a download. A digest sent alongside a message can be
recomputed by anyone.

CRYPTOGRAPHY ALGORITHMS AT A GLANCE
Authenticated and public-key encryption
Authenticated encryption (AE) hides the message and detects tampering. Public-key encryption
lets anyone encrypt for the private-key holder.
Authenticated encryption
Encrypt-then-MAC
Encrypts the message and tags the ciphertext with a separate key. Verify the
tag before decrypting and cover any IV or nonce that affects decryption.
Encrypt-and-MAC
Encrypts the message and sends a separate tag over the plaintext. The
visible tag can leak information in some constructions.
MAC-then-Encrypt
Tags the plaintext and encrypts the message and tag together. Security
depends on the specific construction and its checks.
GCM / AES-GCM
Uses CTR for encryption and GHASH for authentication. Repeating a nonce
under the same key can compromise secrecy and tag security.
CCM
Combines CBC-MAC for authentication with CTR mode for encryption.
EAX
Combines CTR encryption with OMAC, a block-cipher-based tag, to
authenticate the nonce, header and ciphertext.
ChaCha20-Poly1305
Uses ChaCha20 for encryption and Poly1305 for authentication.
AEAD
Authenticated encryption with associated data. Encrypts the message and
authenticates both the message and public metadata, such as a header.
Public-key encryption and RSA
TDF / TDP
A trapdoor function is easy to compute publicly and hard to reverse without
the private key. A trapdoor permutation also shuffles a fixed domain
one-to-one.
TDF hybrid encryption
Protects a fresh random value with the public-key operation, hashes that
value into a symmetric key and uses AE for the actual message.
Textbook RSA
Raises the message number to the public exponent modulo N. The private
exponent reverses it. Direct use is deterministic and malleable.
RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 encryption
Adds random padding and a 00 02 format marker before RSA. Leaking
padding validity creates the Bleichenbacher padding-oracle risk.
RSA-OAEP
Mixes a random seed and the message using hash-based masks before
RSA encryption. Decryption verifies the structure of the encoding.
MGF
A mask generation function expands a seed into bytes of the required
length. OAEP and PSS use it in their encodings.
AE detects tampering. The receiver needs a separate freshness check to catch replayed messages.
Deck 2, slides 28-43. Deck 3, slides 1-39. ChaCha20-Poly1305 is from the course discussion.

CRYPTOGRAPHY ALGORITHMS AT A GLANCE
Key exchange, signatures and derivation
Key exchange establishes a shared secret. Signatures authenticate messages. A key derivation
function turns one secret into keys for specific uses.
Key establishment
Online TTP / Kerberos
A trusted third party distributes session keys. Kerberos uses tickets to
deliver credentials.
DH / ECDH
Diffie-Hellman lets both sides combine their private value with the other
side’s public value to get the same secret. ECDH uses elliptic-curve points.
DHE / ECDHE
Uses fresh private values for each exchange. With authentication and proper
handling of temporary keys, this can provide forward secrecy.
Public-key key transport
One side chooses fresh secret material and encrypts it to the other side’s
public key. The recipient decrypts it.
GNFS / Shor’s algorithm
GNFS is a classical algorithm for factoring large integers. Shor’s quantum
algorithm solves factoring and discrete logarithms given a sufficiently
capable quantum computer.
Digital signatures
Hash-and-sign
Hashes the message first and signs the digest with a private key. Anyone
with the authentic public key can verify the signature.
Full Domain Hash (FDH)
Hashes the message into the full trapdoor-permutation domain, then applies
the private inverse. Verification applies the public operation and compares
hashes.
RSA PKCS#1 v1.5 signatures
Encodes the digest and hash algorithm identifier with a 00 01 marker before
applying the RSA private operation.
RSA-PSS
Uses a random salt and a hash-based mask before RSA signing. The same
message can have several valid signatures.
DSA / ECDSA
DSA uses modular arithmetic and relies on discrete-log hardness. ECDSA
uses elliptic-curve arithmetic. Both create digital signatures.
Key derivation
PRF-based KDF
Starts from a uniform secret and uses different context labels or counters to
derive keys for different jobs or traffic directions.
HKDF
Uses HMAC in two stages. Extract turns sufficiently unpredictable input into
a pseudorandom key. Expand derives keys using context labels.
PBKDF2
Derives a key from a password. A salt makes outputs specific to the
instance, and repeated work raises the cost of each guess.
Authenticate DH to prevent impersonation. OAEP is for RSA encryption. PSS is for RSA signatures.
Deck 3, slides 38-39. Deck 4, slides 3-37.
